cia-0000119211:
From about January 1985, this CIA document concerns reports that American prisoners of war were executed during the 1970s. Claims like these were the darkest the agency had to weigh in its missing-persons work. The paper preserves the allegation together with the agency's handling of it.

Judging such reports meant sorting rumor, faulty memory, and possible fact. A claim of executions, if true, changed both history and policy, and if false, it could torment families for nothing. The document shows that weighing process at work. It stands as part of the record of how the government treated the hardest questions left by the war.
cia-0000119711:
An October 1953 CIA paper forecasts probable developments in Iran through 1954. It was written two months after the coup that drove out Prime Minister Mossadegh and restored the Shah's power. Washington now had to judge what the new order would bring.

The paper looks ahead at Iran's politics and at the stability of a government America had helped install. Forecasts made just after a coup carry a special interest, since they show what the winners expected and feared. For readers, this estimate is a check on those hopes: a statement of where Iran seemed bound, made when the Shah's long second reign was only beginning.
cia-0000124311: A July 1951 CIA document reports on American prisoners held at North Korean camps. The camps along the Yalu River held large numbers of men in harsh conditions. What happened inside them became one of the war's lasting disputes, and the paper records the agency's picture. Camp reporting built slowly from escapees, repatriated sick men, and letters, and papers like this one mark stages in assembling a picture long kept deliberately dark.
cia-0000132311:
Kuwaiti oil fires and the major threat they posed fill Situation Report 621 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series. The report is dated February 6, 1991. Hundreds of wells were burning at once. Smoke from the fires choked much of the region and darkened the daytime sky.

The report assesses what the fires threatened most. Health, weather, water supplies, and shipping all stood at risk. So did the hard work of putting the wells out once fighting stopped. The burning fields became one of the war's most lasting images around the world. Readers get the agency's judgment, made while the fires still raged, of how serious the damage could become.
cia-0000132611: Cuba alone fills part three of a CIA item dated July 1, 1960. The section is headed the West. In that section Cuba stood as the standing headline through 1960, needing no further label. A single word carried the whole Cuba file for that day. The short item preserves the entry exactly as the series labeled it.
cia-0000135911: A CIA cable dated 5 May 1954 deals with the true story, in the cable's own words, in files since declassified. The paper sits inside the CIA drive against President Arbenz, run under the code name PBSUCCESS and crowned by the June 1954 coup. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000137011: Meet with the ambassador, SKILLET proposes in this July 1954 cable. It asks the Guatemala City station to discuss a conference with JMBLUG. The ambassador hopes the station will do this. He wants the station to press him at a 23 July conference. A fragment notes he failed to mention something in a referenced message. un-ga-res-11:
What should the first Secretary-General of the United Nations be paid? Resolution 11, passed on 24 January 1946, fixes the terms of the post. The pay must be high enough to draw a person of rank and skill. It must also let him keep the standing of the job, in view of the heavy load the Charter lays on the role.

The wage is set to yield a net 20,000 U.S. dollars. A grant of 20,000 more covers the costs of the role, and a furnished house is kept up by the UN. The first term runs five years. At its end, a second term of five years stands open.
un-ga-res-3411:
South Africa's apartheid regime drew a pledge of support for its foes in Resolution 3411, adopted by the General Assembly on 28 November 1975. The vote came as the UN marked its thirtieth year. The text recalls the long chain of Assembly votes condemning apartheid. It rests on the pledges of the Charter and of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

The Assembly proclaims a special duty. The UN and the world at large owe that duty to the oppressed people of South Africa and to their liberation movements. The same duty runs to those jailed for the fight. The brave struggle of the people, and the heavy price they paid, are praised in plain terms.
un-ga-res-a-69-11: Joint work with the Shanghai Cooperation Organization fills Resolution A/69/11, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The bloc, which links China, Russia, and Central Asian states, has held observer status at the Assembly since 2004. Past votes of 2009, 2010, and 2012 framed the tie, and the two bodies' staffs signed a joint pledge in April 2010. The bloc is called a key regional player on safety in its part of the world.
un-sc-res-111:
Resolution 111 deals with an attack by Israeli regular forces on Syrian forces inside Syria on 11 December 1955. The text was adopted on 19 January 1956, though the catalog record gives 1955. The vote was eight to two, with Iran abstaining. UN truce reports said the attack broke the Israel-Syria armistice deal and crossed the demilitarized zone.

The Council also notes Syrian interference with Israeli activity on Lake Tiberias, which broke the armistice terms as well. It holds that this interference in no way justified the Israeli attack. The resolution is one of a run of Council rulings from these years that tried to keep the 1949 armistice lines from sliding into open war.
un-sc-res-1411: In the sequence of Security Council decisions, Resolution 1411 is the entry catalogued for 2002 in this library. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations.
un-sc-res-1511:
Resolution 1511, adopted in October 2003, gave legal cover to the foreign forces then occupying Iraq. The United States led a multinational force, but its authority needed the Council's backing. The members authorized the force to take all needed steps to keep security.

The text also urges countries to send troops and money, backs an Iraqi Governing Council timetable toward elections, and expands the UN's own role where safety allowed. Coming months after Resolution 1483, it completed the legal frame for postwar Iraq. Readers see occupation policy being rebuilt as shared international business.
un-sc-res-1611:
On July 7, 2005, bombs tore through London's trains and a bus, killing 52 people. The Security Council answered the same day with Resolution 1611. In it, the members condemn the attacks without reserve and send sympathy to the victims' families.

The text urges every country to help Britain bring the bombers, their planners, and their backers to justice. It repeats the Council's view that terrorism is a threat to peace everywhere, whatever its claimed cause. Brief and direct, the resolution is the world's formal voice speaking in the first hours after an attack.
un-sc-res-1811: Resolution 1811 is a formal act of the Security Council, preserved here in the wording of the UN's official record via Wikisource. The document speaks once, as a body, after negotiation among fifteen delegations. That single voice, with its findings and its numbered decisions, is the content of the entry, kept complete for reference and citation.
un-sc-res-2011: Resolution 2011 is a formal act of the fifteen-member Security Council, preserved here in official-record wording through Wikisource. Its paragraphs were drafted to be implemented by people who were not in the room, which is why they spell out duties so plainly. The entry preserves that plain spelling entire, from first finding to last instruction.
cia-0000132511: February 4, 1961 brought yet another CIA briefing titled simply Cuba. cia-0000136611: An estimated date of 4 November 1960 heads this Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade files, with the estimate flagged in the catalog title. plos-pone-0000011:
Matthew Falagas, Konstantinos Fragoulis, and Ioannis Karydis compared drug prices across medicine in a 2006 PLOS ONE study. New antibiotics draw special worry: bacteria keep evolving resistance, so fresh ones are badly needed, yet firms say developing them pays poorly. The authors asked whether new antibiotics actually cost more than new drugs in other fields.

They set the price of new antibiotics beside drugs from other therapeutic categories, from heart medicine to cancer care. Price gaps, where they exist, feed the debate over why so few antibiotics reach the market. The comparison gives policy makers a factual base for arguments about incentives, patents, and the true cost of staying ahead of resistant germs.
cia-0000137111: An estimated-date 1961 Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade papers; the catalog gives only the year and marks it as estimated. The Brigade was the CIA-trained Cuban exile force that landed at the Bay of Pigs in April 1961. The record names no subject or month for this item. It is preserved in the original Spanish in the declassified release, a loosely dated piece of the brigade's final-year archive.
cia-0000137411: Spanish paperwork from Brigade 2506 fills document 0000137411, dated to 1961 with the date itself marked as an estimate. The brigade was the exile unit the CIA built for the Bay of Pigs, and much of its internal writing stayed in the men's own language. No subject line comes with this record, so its precise business is left to the page itself. It stands as one small piece of a failed invasion's archive, now open to any reader.
husserl-philosophie-als-strenge-wissensc:
Edmund Husserl published his essay Philosophy as Rigorous Science in the journal Logos in 1911, and the German text is given here. Husserl taught at Göttingen and had founded phenomenology, a method that studies how things appear to the mind. The essay served as a public call to rebuild philosophy on firm ground.

Two foes draw his fire: the view that thought is just brain work for science to explain, and the view that truth shifts with each age. Both, he argued, end in doubt about all knowledge. His fix was a strict method that sets aside rash claims and studies experience itself. The piece set the course for much of later European thought.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d11: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on June 20, 1943, two days after the president's paired letters to London and Moscow. His message is Document 11 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The summer correspondence between the two men ran at a pace that matched the war itself. What this note carried, the catalog does not say. It survives in the Foreign Relations series as one link in the long exchange behind the autumn summits.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d111: Roosevelt wrote to Chiang Kai-shek on November 10, 1943, his last letter to China's leader in this series before the journey. It is Document 111 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The Cairo Conference opened twelve days later. The record supplies the date and the names and leaves the subject to the text. The letter is part of the Foreign Relations series' account of how the Cairo meeting was arranged.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d211:
Ambassador Averell Harriman sent President Roosevelt a secret cable from Moscow on 11 November 1943, numbered SD 1. He warns that a thorny subject is almost sure to come up at the coming conference: Soviet pressure on Sweden to help in the war. Molotov had raised the point more than once since the Moscow conference ended.

Harriman reports a talk with Sweden's minister in Moscow. Finland, the minister said, would quit the war quickly if sure Soviet troops would not occupy her afterward, and Sweden could feed Finland for six months once German shipments stopped. But he doubted Sweden could move either Moscow or Helsinki in time, and he noted the Swedish king hoped to spare his people the suffering of joining the war.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d311:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote a most-secret memorandum at Cairo on 25 November 1943 attacking the American plan for a supreme commander over the war against Germany. He sets out, point by point, why the appointment would not cure the troubles seen since the Salerno landing.

The real divergences, Churchill argues, are political as much as military. Only governments and the Combined Chiefs can settle them. A supreme commander would thus be squeezed into a narrow strip of work, or else supplant the chiefs entirely. No single officer, he doubts, could decide across so vast a range. His own rule is that command in each theater should go to the ally with the largest forces there: the Mediterranean British, Overlord American. A merged command, by force counts, would fall to a Briton, an outcome he calls invidious and refuses to impose.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d411:
The agreed text of the Tehran communiqué, is dated 4 December 1943. It is the version Churchill and Stalin accepted. It is printed with its handwritten deletions, and with Harriman's note in the corner of the single sheet. An editorial headnote explains how this copy differs from both the third draft and the text finally released.

The text is headed Declaration of the Three Powers. It is timed for release at eight in the evening, Moscow time, on 6 December. It declares the three nations' determination to work together in war and in the peace that follows. Complete agreement was reached on the scope and timing of operations from the east, west, and south. The leaders claim the supreme responsibility of making a peace. The peace must command the good will of the overwhelming mass of the world's peoples. They close as friends in fact, in spirit, and in purpose.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d511:
Charles E. Bohlen, first secretary at the American embassy in Moscow, wrote this memorandum dated December 1, 1943, the final day of the Tehran Conference. Bohlen spoke Russian and served as President Roosevelt's interpreter with Stalin, taking notes at talks where no other American record was made. The State Department printed his memorandum in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Bohlen's papers are prized because he sat between the leaders, hearing both languages at moments that shaped the postwar world. A memorandum from the last day of Tehran carries the closeness of that seat. For readers, it offers the conference through the eyes of the man who made its conversations possible.

arxiv-2606-05211: The Euclidean algorithm — the ancient recipe for greatest common divisors — turns out to illuminate the geometry of singularities, the points where curves go wrong. Edward FitzGerald's 1859 free translation made the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam among the most quoted verses in English. Khayyam was a Persian astronomer and mathematician; tradition credits him with quatrains, four-line poems, spoken in a skeptical, wine-toasting voice. FitzGerald reshaped selected quatrains into a loose sequence that English readers adopted as one poem.

Wine, roses, and the fleeting hour are urged against the certainty of death and the silence beyond it. Scholars argue over how much is Khayyam and how much FitzGerald, and the argument itself is part of the book's history. As seize-the-day wisdom from medieval Persia in Victorian dress, it remains irresistible.
tob-4311:
Valmiki is the name linked to the Yoga-Vasishtha, a huge Sanskrit work of wisdom teaching. Volume one of four, in Vihari-Lala Mitra's translation, opens a long talk between the sage Vasishtha and Prince Rama. Rama is young, troubled by the world, and full of questions about life and death.

Vasishtha answers through stories, arguments, and vivid images. He teaches that the world is shaped by mind, that desire binds people to illusion, and that clear knowledge brings freedom. The teaching unfolds slowly, with tales inside tales. It stands among the longest and deepest works of Hindu thought.
tob-0011:
One hundred fourteen sayings, and nothing else, make up the Gospel of Thomas. A complete copy in Coptic came to light at Nag Hammadi in Egypt in 1945. No birth story, no miracles, no cross: only the voice of Jesus, teaching in short, sharp lines.

Some sayings match the known Gospels; others sound strange and new. The most quoted promises that the kingdom is inside the hearer and all around, yet people do not see it. Scholars argue over the book's date and sources to this day. The evidence notes no public-domain translation is attached yet. The sayings alone explain the fame.
tob-0111:
A. E. Waite, the English occult scholar, restored the Hermetic Museum to print with his own English versions of classic alchemical tracts. The set first appeared in Latin in 1678, gathering works like the Golden Tripod and Sendivogius's New Light of Alchemy. Waite's edition carries his commentary throughout.

He treats alchemy as a spiritual discipline as much as a laboratory art, a view that shaped his whole career. The Victorian revival of alchemy speaks with his voice in this volume. Verified from a pre-1930 edition, the Museum remains a standard shelf of the old tracts, with Waite as a learned, opinionated guide.
tob-4011:
Giambattista della Porta of Naples filled twenty books with the wonders of Natural Magick, first in 1558 and enlarged for decades. The English version here rests on a verified 1919 public-domain edition. Porta ran an academy of secrets and tested marvels with boyish delight.

Optics, magnetism, distillation, invisible writing, and strange gardening all get hands-on treatment. Some recipes work, some amuse, and a few alarm. For two centuries the book was a household favorite across Europe, reprinted again and again. It shows the age when science and magic had not yet parted, and when experiment itself still felt like a marvel.
tob-4111:
Ralph T. H. Griffith turned the Rigveda into flowing English verse, and volume one holds the first half of his translation. Griffith, a scholar in India, aimed to make the oldest hymns of India sing for Victorian readers. Agni, Indra, and the gods of storm and dawn lead the collection.

Famous creation hymns ask who really knows how the world began, a note of honest doubt amid the praise. Sacrifice, battle, and prayer shape the rest. Griffith's meter carries lines that prose versions flatten. Verified from the 1919 edition, volume one shows why his Rigveda outsang every rival of its century.
tob-10111:
Cyprian, bishop of Carthage in North Africa, wrote On the Unity of the Church in the third century, after fierce persecution had split his church. Some Christians who had lapsed under torture wanted back in, and rival bishops claimed power.

Cyprian argues that the church is one body and that no one can hold faith apart from its bishops and its shared life. His famous claim, that outside the church there is no salvation, shaped Catholic teaching on the church for centuries. The short treatise still anchors debates about unity, authority, and schism.
tob-0039-d11:
Roll 16 is a later reel of the Doctors' Trial microfilm, the verbatim record of the Nuremberg case of 1946 to 1947. By this point the proceedings against the Nazi physicians were far advanced. The transcript keeps the trial day by day, without summary.

Further testimony and exhibits enter the record here as prosecution and defense press their cases toward judgment. The defendants included doctors who had run camp experiments and officials who oversaw them. Kept entire and unedited, the rolls let any reader check later histories against the source. This reel continues the archive that documents how the trial built toward its verdicts and its medical code.
govdocs-archive_org-TheSpotlightVolume27:
The Spotlight was a populist weekly newspaper published in Washington, and this file holds a single issue: volume 27, number 11, dated March 12, 2001. Single issues are kept as issued, so the paper can be read exactly as its subscribers saw it.

Inside are the paper's news stories, commentary, and notes from its own distinct perspective, which favored economic nationalism and deep suspicion of global institutions. The Spotlight spoke to readers who distrusted the mainstream press, and it kept a loyal following for decades. As a record, the issue shows what that audience was reading in the spring of 2001.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-11:
Volume eleven of Rodkinson's Babylonian Talmud holds the first part of Tract Baba Metzia, the Middle Gate. Baba Metzia is the Talmud's richest field of everyday civil law. Its cases come from markets, workshops, and shared courtyards across the rabbinic world.

The tractate opens with two men clutching one cloak, each swearing it is his: the court must split the claim. From there it runs through found goods, deposits left with a keeper, wages owed to laborers, and loans and interest. Rodkinson's notes flag the hardest turns in the debate. Business readers meet an ancient law of trade that still feels alive.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-11:
Volume eleven of Schaff's Nicene Fathers, first series, holds Chrysostom's homilies on the Acts of the Apostles and on the Epistle to the Romans. The volume dates from 1886. Chrysostom preached the Acts series near the end of his time in Constantinople.

The Acts homilies follow the apostles from Jerusalem outward, with Chrysostom marveling at their boldness and shaming his own softer age. The Romans homilies then work through Paul's hardest letter, untangling faith, law, and grace for lay hearers. His praise of Paul runs through both series like a refrain. The volume pairs the church's first story with its first theology, preached by its greatest preacher.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-11:
Volume eleven of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890, joins Sulpitius Severus, Vincent of Lerins, and John Cassian. The three are the voices of early western monasticism. Schaff and Wace edited the series.

Sulpitius wrote the life of Martin of Tours, the soldier-saint whose cloak, shared with a beggar, became legend. Vincent's Commonitory gives the famous rule for telling old faith from new error: what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all. Cassian's conferences then carry the wisdom of Egypt's desert monks to the West, on prayer, purity, and grace. The volume shaped how western monks lived and prayed for centuries.
frus-1961-1963-cuban-missile-crisis-vol-:
Volume eleven of Foreign Relations of the United States for 1961 to 1963 is devoted to the Cuban Missile Crisis and its aftermath. The Office of the Historian compiled it from declassified records. For thirteen days in October 1962, the world stood at the edge of nuclear war.

The documents follow the Executive Committee's secret debates as Kennedy weighed invasion, air strikes, and blockade. The naval quarantine, the downed U-2, and the near accidents at sea all stand in the record. Behind the public standoff runs the secret deal: Soviet missiles out of Cuba, American missiles quietly out of Turkey. The volume is the crisis in its makers' own words.
waite-pictorial-key-to-the-tarot-1911:
Arthur Edward Waite gave the modern tarot its fixed face and book in 1911. The Pictorial Key to the Tarot explains the deck he devised with the artist Pamela Colman Smith. That deck, the Rider-Waite, is the one most readers still learn on.

Waite tells the lore of the cards, then walks through each trump and suit card in turn. He gives the meanings he held true and scorns mere fortune-telling tricks. His readings stress sign and soul over luck and dread. For a century, tarot study has run in the channel this book cut.
blackwood-centaur-1911:
Algernon Blackwood turned from ghost tales to a tale of faith in The Centaur, his novel of 1911. A man who feels trapped by town life sails and walks in search of a truer world. In the hills he meets hints that old myths still live.

The tale claims that earth holds a deep shared soul. The last centaurs stand for a pure bond with wild life. Blackwood pours his love of woods and hills into the prose. It is the peak of his tales of awe in wild places. Some fans find its creed dense. Yet its love for green hills and clean air rings true, and its quest has real ache in it.
james-more-ghost-stories-1911:
More lore and more curses fill M. R. James's next set of ghost tales, from 1911. Its best known tale sends a curse by runes on a scrap of paper. A proud man who spurned a scholar's work finds dread dogging each step he takes.

James keeps his dry wit and slow build. Old halls, inns, and church tombs hide each threat. Facts pile up till doubt fails. The set shows his craft at full strength. It fixed his name as the chief of the form. A lost maze, a cursed inn, and a school tale with a grim well fill the set. Each shows James at ease with pace, lore, and shock.
onions-widdershins-1911:
Oliver Onions filled Widdershins, his set of tales from 1911, with ghosts that gnaw at the mind. Its most famed tale lures a painter to a flat where a fair voice calls. The flat holds him. Art, love, and dread blur till he can't break free.

Onions writes with care and a slow, sure hand. Fear grows from mood and small signs, not shocks. The set is a high mark of ghost tales from its age. Its lead tale is oft called the best house tale. Onions had a deft hand for folk who drift and dream. His ghosts prey on that drift, which makes the scares feel close and sad.
hill-new-evidences-psychical-research-19:
J. Arthur Hill adds fresh proof to the pile in New Evidences in Psychical Research, his book of 1911. Hill was a keen hand in the chief band for such study. He prints his own tests. Sittings with seers sit by tales that checked out true. Some talks seemed to come from the dead through more than one voice in far towns.

His tone is calm, fair, and shorn of wild zeal. He asks fans to weigh, not to swoon. The book is a fair flag of the field in its prime age. It shows its care at work.
chrystal-perpetual-motion-1911:
George Chrystal, a Scots scholar of maths and physics, wrote this survey of perpetual motion for the Encyclopaedia Britannica in 1911. By then the laws of heat and work had long since closed the case. Chrystal set out the full tale for the lay reader.

He walks from the old wheel schemes to the strict proof that no such machine can work. He notes the French Academy's ban of 1775, when it shut its doors to all such claims. The piece is the learned world's last word on the long dream. It can be read in full in a short, clear sitting.
boule-la-chapelle-aux-saints-1911:
Marcellin Boule, a French sage of fossil man, wrote this memoir in French on the La Chapelle-aux-Saints find in 1911. Quarry men in France had found a near whole Neanderthal frame in a cave in 1908. Boule got the bones for his full study in Paris.

His rebuild of the man stooped, bent at the knees, with a brutish, ape like gait. That image of the Neanderthal as a dull brute held sway for some forty years in books and museums. Later work showed the frame was bent by age and joint pain, not by race.
keith-ancient-types-of-man-1911:
Arthur Keith, a Scots doctor and sage of man's rise, wrote this plain survey of fossil man in 1911. It was made for the lay reader, with clear plates and a brisk pace. Keith was then one of the best known names in the field in Britain.

He walks from the Neanderthal and Piltdown finds to the frames of Gibraltar and Java. His famed rebuild of the Gibraltar skull shows his hand at the craft of the time. The book taught a whole age the tale of fossil man as its chief men then told it.
selenka-pithecanthropus-schichten-java-1:
Emil Selenka planned a great dig in Java to restudy the beds where Dubois found his ape man. He died before the trip, and his wife led the work in his name. Max Blanckenhorn joined her, and their joint memoir came out in German in 1911.

The team dug the Trinil beds once more and set out their rocks and beast bones in full. Their work tests where the ape man's bones lay and what age the beds must bear. The book is the first full site study of the most famed find in the field.
fouque-undine-1811:
Friedrich de la Motte Fouque, a German officer and writer, wrote this tale of a water spirit in 1811. F. E. Bunnett turned it into English, in the full text of nineteen parts. The tale grew from old lore of the undine, the maid of the waters.

Undine is raised by a fisherman, weds a knight, and by that bond wins a human soul. Joy turns to grief as the knight fails her, and the waters call her back at last. The short tale fixed the form of the water spirit in the books of Europe.
heindel-rosicrucian-mysteries-1911:
Max Heindel put out The Rosicrucian Mysteries in 1911. The book is a plain first step into the scheme of the Rosicrucian Fellowship. Heindel had set up that group in the United States not long past. He calls the book a first exposition, made for new hands.

Seven worlds stack up in his scheme, from dense flesh to pure spirit. Man has more than one body in his count, and death is a shift, not an end. Steps of growth lead the soul to full sight of hid things. The book is the gate text of Heindel's whole school.
sepharial-manual-occultism-1911:
Sepharial was the pen name of Walter Gorn Old, a famed occult scribe. His Manual of Occultism came out in 1911. The book packs the whole field of hid arts in one stout tome. It was made as a desk book for the keen new hand.

Star lore, palm lines, name sums, and seals each get a short course. Ways to tell fate by cards, lots, and signs fill the last parts. Sepharial writes in a brisk, plain hand with no wasted words. The book is a fine snap shot of the occult trade in its Edwardian prime.
ibn-arabi-tarjuman-1911:
Ibn Arabi was the great Sufi sage of Spain and the East. His Tarjuman al-Ashwaq, the Interpreter of Desires, holds his love poems. R. A. Nicholson turned them into English in 1911, with the Arab text at hand. A young woman of Mecca first woke the poems in him.

On their face, the odes praise her grace in rich, warm lines. Ibn Arabi then adds his own notes to bare the hid sense. Each grace, he says, points to God and the soul's love for Him. The book is a core text of Sufi thought on love.
evans-wentz-fairy-faith-1911:
W. Y. Evans-Wentz walked the Celt lands to ask folk what they held on fays. The Fairy-Faith in Celtic Countries came out in 1911. He went through Ireland, Scotland, Wales, Cornwall, Brittany, and Man. Old men and women told him what their kin had seen and feared.

First-hand tales fill the book: troops of fays, hid folk, and stolen babes. Evans-Wentz then weighs what the tales may mean for the mind and soul. He treats the faith with care, not with scorn. The book is the base work for all grave study of fay lore.
wells-country-of-blind-and-other-stories:
H. G. Wells put out The Country of the Blind, and Other Stories in 1911. The book holds a long run of his short tales from the years past. Its title tale is one of his most famed works. A lost range in the Andes hides a vale where all are blind.

A climber falls into the vale and thinks he can rule the blind folk. Their touch and ear prove sharp past his sight, and his plans fail. The Empire of the Ants tells of ants that learn war and sweep up a river land. The set is a strong late store of Wells's short art.
austen-sense-and-sensibility-1811:
Jane Austen published Sense and Sensibility in 1811, her first novel in print. The story tracks the Dashwood sisters after their father's death strips their income. Elinor stands for sense, and Marianne for open, strong feeling in love and grief.

Both sisters fall in love, and both face loss, gossip, and hard reversals. Marianne's romance with Willoughby ends in public shame and deep illness at Cleveland. Elinor hides her own pain while she nurses her sister back to health. Austen weighs heart and reason without mocking either side of the scale. The prose is crisp, ironic, and quietly fond of its flawed young women.
ibsen-a-dolls-house-sharp-1911:
Henrik Ibsen wrote A Doll's House in Norwegian, and R. Farquharson Sharp made this Dent version in 1911. The play detonated modern drama when its last scene first stunned audiences in Copenhagen and beyond. Nora's door slam at the end was heard, as the phrase goes, round the world.

Nora Helmer seems a gay, childish wife in a snug and prosperous bourgeois home. A secret loan and a forged name rise to threaten her husband's new bank post. Torvald's rage at the scandal shows Nora she has lived as a doll, not a person. She walks out on husband and children to find herself, in a shocking close. The play still sparks debate on marriage, duty, and a woman's right to selfhood.
nietzsche-twilight-idols-ludovici-1911:
Friedrich Nietzsche published Twilight of the Idols in 1889, a short summary of his mature thought. The English text here is Anthony M. Ludovici's translation of 1911. Nietzsche said he wrote it as a rest between larger works. Its subtitle calls it how to philosophize with a hammer.

Short sections strike at Socrates, German culture, morality, and metaphysics in turn. Famous maxims open the book, including what does not kill me makes me stronger. Nietzsche tests old idols by tapping them for hollow sounds. The style is fast, funny, and cutting. It is one of the best short entries into his thought.
bergson-creative-evolution-mitchell-1911:
Henri Bergson published Creative Evolution in 1907, a French work of philosophy about life and change. The English text here is Arthur Mitchell's translation of 1911. Bergson sets the elan vital, a vital impulse driving life forward, against cold mechanism. Evolution, he argues, creates new forms in ways no machine model can capture.

He criticizes both Darwinian mechanism and fixed final goals. Intellect, he says, slices living flow into static parts, while intuition grasps it whole. The book was a sensation and won Bergson worldwide fame. It shaped process thought and much art of its era. Many call it the most influential philosophy of life of its century.
bergson-matter-memory-paul-1911:
Henri Bergson published Matter and Memory in 1896, a French study of mind and body. The English text here is the 1911 translation by Nancy Margaret Paul and W. Scott Palmer. Bergson asks how memory joins the material world. He argues that memory is not stored in the brain like goods in a box.

He distinguishes habit memory, held in the body, from pure memory of the past. Perception, for him, selects images for action rather than copying the world. The book attacks materialism while respecting science. It founded much modern philosophy of mind. Thinkers on time, self, and brain science still engage its claims.
bergson-laughter-brereton-1911:
Henri Bergson published Laughter in 1900, a short French essay on why we laugh. The English text here is the 1911 translation by Cloudesley Brereton and Fred Rothwell. Bergson argues that laughter targets rigidity in people. We laugh when a living person acts like a stiff machine or a thing.

Comedy, he says, works as a social correction that shames inelastic habits. The comic figure is often vain, absent-minded, or stuck in a groove. Bergson studies farce, caricature, and wordplay for support. The theory is elegant and still widely taught. Later theories of humor often start by answering Bergson.
zimmern-greek-commonwealth-1911:
Alfred Zimmern published The Greek Commonwealth in 1911, a portrait of Athens in the 400s BC. Zimmern treats politics, economy, and thought as parts of one whole. The polis, or city-state, is his central subject. Pericles' Athens stands at the height of its power and art.

He explains farms, trade, slaves, festivals, and assemblies in plain terms. Thucydides serves as his chief guide and hero. Zimmern wrote for students and general readers, not only specialists. The book became the classic English portrait of fifth-century Athens. Its warm liberal faith in the city-state reflects its age. Later scholarship revised details, yet the whole still charms and instructs.
cumont-oriental-religions-showerman-1911:
Franz Cumont's The Oriental Religions in Roman Paganism appears in Grant Showerman's translation of 1911. Cumont studies the cults that flowed into Rome from the East. Isis from Egypt, Mithras from Persia, Cybele from Asia Minor, and Syrian gods transformed Roman religion. Their rites promised purity and life after death.

Cumont argues these faiths prepared the way for Christianity's triumph. His synthesis was a masterwork that reshaped the study of Roman religion. Later scholars corrected details, yet his map still guides the field. The lectures read clearly for general audiences. They remain the classic short account of Rome's eastern cults. Showerman's version served English readers well.
boas-mind-primitive-man-1911:
Franz Boas taught at Columbia and is often called the father of American anthropology. His 1911 book The Mind of Primitive Man attacks the claim that some races are born with stronger minds than others. It draws on years of field work and museum study.

Boas shows that race, language, and culture move on separate tracks and must not be confused. A people's tools, tales, and habits, he argues, grow from their history, not from their blood. The book laid the ground for cultural relativism, the view that each culture must be judged on its own terms.
saadi-bustan-hart-edwards-1911:
Saadi, the thirteenth-century Persian poet of Shiraz, wrote the Bustan, meaning The Orchard, as a long poem on right living. Edwards's 1911 English rendering presents the work to modern readers in clear prose form. The Bustan stands as the companion volume to Saadi's famous Gulistan.

Ten chapters treat justice, kindness, humility, love, and the duties of kings and dervishes in turn. Tales of rulers, slaves, and saints carry the lessons, each closed by a pointed moral. For centuries Persian schoolchildren learned ethics and statecraft from these pages, and the poem still anchors Persian moral teaching.
underhill-mysticism-1911:
Underhill's Mysticism, published in 1911, is the epochal study of the nature and growth of man's spiritual consciousness. She wrote it after years of reading the mystics of many lands in their own words. The book defined the modern study of mysticism for the English-speaking world.

Underhill maps the mystic way in stages: awakening, purgation, illumination, the dark night, and the unitive life. She illustrates each stage from Teresa, John of the Cross, Julian, and dozens of lesser-known witnesses. Her mix of scholarship, sympathy, and clear order turned a scattered library into one readable story.
sepharial-kabala-of-numbers-1911:
Sepharial was the pen name of Walter Gorn Old, a Theosophist and astrologer of wide output. His Kabala of Numbers, published in 1911, is a manual of numerology and gematria from the Theosophical era. Gematria assigns numbers to letters and reads names and words by their sums.

Sepharial teaches how to turn a name into its number, judge its force, and apply the same art to dates, places, and events. He draws on Hebrew tradition, Greek practice, and the occult teaching of his own circle. The book served the revival's students as their handbook for the hidden arithmetic of words.
sepharial-second-sight-1911:
Sepharial's Second Sight, published in 1911, studies clairvoyance, the claimed power of seeing what the senses cannot reach. He divides his subject into natural second sight and induced clairvoyance, trained by practice. The book surveys both with an occultist's sympathy and a reporter's care.

Scottish Highland seers, crystal gazers, and modern psychics all pass through his chapters with their cases and claims. Sepharial weighs the evidence for a faculty beyond the five senses and finds much of it, in his judgment, hard to dismiss. The study preserves the period's best case for second sight as its believers made it.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-02-1911:
James George Frazer published Volume 2 of the third edition of The Golden Bough in 1911, subtitled The Magic Art and the Evolution of Kings, Part 2. Frazer, a Cambridge scholar, built his vast study of magic and religion from reports across the world. The third edition ran to twelve volumes.

Part 2 of The Magic Art presses on with charms, rites, and the rise of sacred kings. Frazer argued that magic came before religion in human thought, and that kings began as magicians. His examples range from rain makers to tree spirits on every continent. The volume shows his method at full scale: one custom matched against hundreds of kin worldwide.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-03-1911:
Volume 3 of Frazer's Golden Bough, third edition, appeared in 1911, under the title Taboo and the Perils of the Soul. James George Frazer gathered customs from peoples worldwide to show how taboo worked. Taboo, a word from Polynesia, named things and persons set apart as dangerous and holy.

Chapters cover taboos on kings, strangers, food, words, and the dead, and beliefs about the soul leaving the body in sleep or shadow. Frazer argued that taboo guarded early societies where law did not yet reach. His mass of examples, drawn from travelers and missionaries, made the volume a storehouse for later students of religion, even those who rejected his theories.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-04-1911:
Volume 4 of the third edition of The Golden Bough appeared in 1911, titled The Dying God. James George Frazer's theme was the god who dies and returns, a figure he found in rites across the ancient world. The priest of Nemi, slain by his successor, stood behind the whole work.

Frazer traced dying gods through grain rites, sacred kings, and seasonal festivals in many lands. He held that such rites acted out the death and revival of plant life each year. Critics later doubted his single pattern, but the evidence he gathered stayed valuable. The volume is central to his claim that myth and ritual grow from the same root.
descartes-philosophical-works-haldane-ro:
Elizabeth S Haldane and G R T Ross published Volume 1 of The Philosophical Works of Descartes in 1911. Their translation became the standard English Descartes for most of the twentieth century. René Descartes, the French founder of modern philosophy, wrote the works gathered here across his career.

Volume 1 holds the Rules for the Direction of the Mind, the Discourse on Method, and the Meditations on First Philosophy. Selections from the Principles of Philosophy, The Search after Truth, and The Passions of the Soul follow. Readers meet the cogito, the doubt of the senses, and the split of mind and body in Descartes's own order. No single volume gives a fuller start on him.
schreiner-woman-and-labour-1911:
Olive Schreiner published Woman and Labour in 1911 in London. Schreiner, the South African novelist of The Story of an African Farm, had worked on the book for years and lost a longer draft. The published part became her feminist classic.

Schreiner argued that modern industry had taken women's old work out of the home, leaving leisured women as parasites on men's labor. She demanded that women win back a share in all fields of work, not as a favor but as a right. Her image of the leisured woman, ornamental and dependent, stung readers across the English-speaking world. The book shaped suffrage-era thought on women and work.
conrad-under-western-eyes-1911:
Joseph Conrad, born in Poland under Russian rule, returned to the world of revolutionaries in Under Western Eyes, published in 1911. An English teacher of languages in Geneva tells the story. It is often called Conrad's darkest political novel.

A St. Petersburg student named Razumov shelters an assassin who has just killed a minister. Fearing ruin, Razumov betrays him, then is sent to Geneva as a spy on the exile circle. There he falls in love with the dead man's sister while living his lie. The novel dissects guilt, autocracy, and the blindness of the watching West.
lawrence-white-peacock-1911:
D. H. Lawrence was a young schoolteacher in the Midlands when he wrote The White Peacock. His first novel, it was published in 1911 after years of drafting. Lawrence set it in the countryside around his home town of Eastwood in Nottinghamshire.

Two sisters, Lettie and Meg, move through courtships that go wrong in different ways. Around them, the gamekeeper Annable preaches a rough gospel of the body against polite society. Farming life, poaching, and the pit villages fill the background with rich detail. The novel is uneven and lush, but Lawrence's eye for nature and class tension is already fully alive.
pope-essay-on-criticism-1711:
Alexander Pope was only twenty-three when An Essay on Criticism appeared in 1711. Pope, a Catholic shut out of university and office, had taught himself the classics at home. The poem made his name at once and has never gone out of print.

Written in crisp heroic couplets, the essay teaches how to judge poetry: study nature, learn the ancients, and beware of pride and fashion. Famous lines urge that a little learning is a dangerous thing, and that to err is human, to forgive divine. Generations of writers learned their taste from Pope's manual. It remains the clearest statement of neoclassical poetics in English.
london-south-sea-tales-1911:
Jack London cruised the South Pacific on his yacht Snark in 1907 and 1908, gathering material until illness forced him home. South Sea Tales, published in 1911, holds the fiction that came out of the Solomon Islands and Hawaii. It is his Pacific work at its most brutal and most humane.

The stories confront white traders, missionaries, and planters exploiting island peoples, and islanders answering in kind. One tale visits Molokai's leper colony, where London finds courage and dignity among the outcast sick. Another follows a pearl diver and a hurricane. London neither romanticizes the islands nor excuses the whites. The sea, the heat, and sudden violence rule these pages, told in his hardest prose.
dreiser-jennie-gerhardt-1911:
Theodore Dreiser published Jennie Gerhardt in 1911, eleven years after his first novel was buried by its own publisher. His editors cut the manuscript heavily, fearing its treatment of an unmarried mother. Dreiser based Jennie partly on his own sisters' hard lives in Indiana poverty.

Jennie, a poor laundress in Columbus, is seduced by an aging senator who dies before he can marry her. She then devotes herself to a rich man's son, Lester Kane, living with him outside marriage and sacrificing her happiness to protect his. Dreiser refuses to judge her; his slow, heavy prose builds pity instead. Jennie Gerhardt is his most tender and morally complex novel, and the one many readers love best.
rolland-jean-christophe-cannan-vol2-1911:
Jean-Christophe in Paris forms the second volume of Romain Rolland's great novel cycle, in Gilbert Cannan's translation of 1911. It holds books five through seven: The Market-Place, Antoinette, and The House. Christophe, now a grown composer, leaves Germany and tries his luck in the French capital.

Paris at first dazzles and then disgusts him with its buying and selling of art. He finds true friends, among them the devoted Olivier family, and honors the memory of Antoinette. Work, poverty, and loyalty shape these middle years. Rolland uses the city to test his hero's ideals against the market. The volume deepens the cycle's portrait of the artist in modern Europe.
andreyev-king-hunger-1911:
King Hunger, Leonid Andreyev's allegorical play, appeared in English in Poet Lore in the winter of 1911. Eugene M. Kayden made the translation. King Hunger, a gaunt personified power, rouses the starving poor of a great city to rise against the rich who feast above them.

Bells, judges, and workers people the stark, symbolic stages of the play. The rising swells toward a climax that Andreyev shapes as vision rather than report. He called such works dramas of ideas, meant to stage the forces that move crowds. Of all his plays, this one presses revolution most directly. The Poet Lore printing gave American readers an early taste of his radical theater.
bonaventure-tria-opuscula-1911:
Bonaventure, the Franciscan master who led his order and taught at Paris, wrote three short works that hold his whole thought in seed. The Quaracchi edition of 1911 prints them together in Latin: the Breviloquium, the Itinerarium Mentis in Deum, and the De Reductione Artium ad Theologiam. No complete English version in the public domain exists.

The Breviloquium sums up the whole of theology in seven tight parts. The Itinerarium leads the soul up six steps, through the world and the mind, to rest in God. The third piece shows how every art and science leads back to theology. Together they are the handbook of Franciscan thought at its height.
zohar-de-pauly-french-vol-6-1911:
Jean de Pauly finished his French Zohar in 1911 with this sixth tome. The Zohar, the Book of Splendor, is the supreme work of the Kabbalah, an Aramaic commentary on the Torah ascribed to the school of Moses de Leon. De Pauly's six tomes form the only complete translation of it in the public domain.

The closing tome brings the long commentary to its end, with the last portions of the Torah read as maps of the divine life. Rabbi Shimon and his companions have by now taught a whole cosmos: God in ten lights, Israel in exile, and the world awaiting repair. De Pauly's achievement gave the West its first full Zohar. The set stands complete in this volume.
scheible-das-kloster-vol11:
Johann Scheible issued band eleven of Das Kloster in 1849, holding cells forty-one through forty-four. Only one band now stood between this one and the end of the great set. The anthology's German subtitle, worldly and spiritual, had proved true in every sense.

Spell books and grimoires fill these cells, with Faust books and Höllenzwänge in close attendance. Folk charms, passed down in speech and scrap print, gain firm type at last. The chapbooks, too, keep coming, tales and wonders from the cheap stalls. Band eleven shows Scheible's stock unthinned near the close: the rescue of old print still ran at full pace.
eucken-truth-religion-1911:
What truth does religion hold, and where does that truth rest? Rudolf Eucken, the 1908 Nobel laureate from Jena, took up both questions in Der Wahrheitsgehalt der Religion in 1901. W. Tudor Jones translated the work, and the text here follows the second edition of 1913.

Eucken argues that religion speaks to the deepest layer of human life, the life of the spirit. He tests rival views of faith and sets out the ground on which belief can stand. His case ties religion to moral effort and inner renewal. The book forms a key part of his philosophy of religion.
ward-realm-ends-1911:
Gifford Lectures again gave James Ward his platform in The Realm of Ends, published in 1911. The subtitle joins its two themes: pluralism and theism. Ward pictured the world as a realm of many free agents, each with its own ends. That picture stood against any single force ruling all.

Across the lectures he asks how many centers of life can form one moral world. God, in his account, works with free beings rather than moving them like tools. He draws on science and on daily moral experience alike. The book states his mature system in full. It rewards readers patient with big questions.
cannizzaro-sketch-chemical-philosophy-19:
Stanislao Cannizzaro's Sketch of a Course of Chemical Philosophy began as his 1858 Italian Sunto. The Alembic Club reprinted the English version in 1911 as Reprint number 18. Cannizzaro revived Avogadro's hypothesis, the idea that equal gas volumes hold equal numbers of molecules. Chemists had let that idea sleep for decades.

With it, he showed how to fix atomic weights on one firm scale. His paper reached the Karlsruhe congress of 1860 and spread among its members. The atomic weight chaos that had plagued chemistry soon ended. The short sketch changed how every chemist reckoned. It reads as a letter that reset a science.
hobhouse-liberalism-1911:
L. T. Hobhouse set out the new liberalism in Liberalism, a compact book of 1911. Older liberal thought had stressed freedom from state meddling above all. Hobhouse argues that real freedom needs food, schooling, and fair terms of work. The state, used with care, becomes a tool of liberty rather than its foe.

He traces liberal ideas from early toleration to his own social program. Each stage widens the circle of who counts as fully free. The book became the classic statement of social liberalism's case for state action. British reform in his century ran on lines he helped draw. It remains a clear, brief classic.
rousseau-emile-foxley-1911:
Rousseau raised a child on paper in Émile, the treatise-novel Barbara Foxley translated for the Everyman line in 1911. Émile grows up guided by nature rather than books, learning from things themselves and from the results of his own acts. Schooling, Rousseau argues, mostly ruins what nature builds well in a child.

One long section, the Profession of Faith of the Savoyard Vicar, sets out a simple, heartfelt creed of its own. That passage helped get the book condemned at its birth, even as its teaching on childhood spread across Europe. Modern ideas of childhood and learning still trace lines back to Émile's pages.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol11:
After a gap in printing, Volume XI of the Journal of Discourses appeared at Liverpool in 1867. Brigham Young and his fellow leaders fill its pages with sermons taken down as spoken. The church they led had weathered war years and kept building, and the pulpit voice here sounds settled and sure.

Doctrine, history, and counsel blend in the talks, aimed at Saints old and new. The Journal's long run lets readers trace how teachings were repeated and reshaped over time. Volume XI resumes that record after the pause, a key link between the early and later sets.
wattles-science-being-great-1911:
Greatness completes Wattles's trilogy in The Science of Being Great, published in 1911 after his death. Getting Rich and Being Well came first; this last book asks what a person should become. Wattles answers that greatness means expressing the advancing mind within, the soul growing into its full size.

He writes for ordinary readers who suspect they were made for more than their present station. Perception, faith, and steady purpose form his path, stated in short, firm chapters. The trilogy's close shows the reach of New Thought ambition: money, health, and character all under one law of thought.
essays-idleness-sansom-1911:
G. B. Sansom Englished Yoshida Kenko's Essays in Idleness in 1911, the first English rendering of the Tsurezuregusa. Kenko, a fourteenth-century courtier turned recluse, set down short pieces as thoughts came to him. Beauty, death, manners, and the folly of ambition drift through his meditations without fixed order.

Kenko loves old things, quiet rooms, and the turning seasons, and distrusts fuss of every kind. His book became one of Japan's most loved classics, a model of the zuihitsu, the follow-the-brush essay. Sansom's translation introduced that gentle art to English readers for the first time.
bleek-lloyd-specimens-of-bushman-folklor:
Wilhelm Bleek and Lucy Lloyd preserved the |Xam people's stories in Specimens of Bushman Folklore, published in 1911. In Cape Town, |Xam men dictated myths, legends, and beliefs to the two scholars over years of patient work. The original |Xam text stands beside the English translation, line for careful line.

The trickster Mantis, the moon, rain, and the early people of the world move through these tales. The speakers' own people and language have since nearly vanished, which makes the record irreplaceable. The volume stands as the founding text of Khoisan ethnography, a whole world saved in notebooks.
mansfield-german-pension-1911:
Katherine Mansfield published this first book in 1911, when she was twenty-two and newly arrived in London from New Zealand. The sketches grew from her stay at a Bavarian spa, taking the waters among German guests she observed with a cold eye.

She skewers the pension's residents: their appetites, vanities, sentimentality, and casual cruelties. The pieces are short, sharp, and funny, with dialogue that pricks like pins. Mansfield later thought the book crude and tried to suppress it. Even so, the voice is already unmistakable: the outsider girl watching, and missing nothing. Her great stories were five years away.
james-some-problems-philosophy-1911:
Some Problems of Philosophy, published in 1911 after James's death, is the unfinished introduction to philosophy he was writing at the end. It is subtitled a beginning of an introduction. The book breaks off mid-course, brought to print by his son's care.

James takes up substance, design, free will, and the quarrel between monism and pluralism. He tests each against his pragmatic method: what difference would the answer make in experience? The writing has his late clarity and charm. Though a fragment, it serves as the best short doorway into his thought. Readers meet the philosopher mid-argument, still working.
james-memories-studies-1911:
Memories and Studies, published in 1911, is a posthumous gathering of James's essays, memorial pieces, and addresses. It shows the philosopher among his dead: teachers, friends, and fellow workers remembered with unusual tenderness.

The volume includes his memorial of Louis Agassiz, his Harvard teacher, and his celebrated address on Emerson. Other pieces take up the moral equivalent of war's themes, the energies of men, and the will to believe's echoes. James writes of persons as he wrote of ideas, with sympathy and precision. The book is the most personal of his volumes, a portrait of a mind through its attachments.
roget-thesaurus-english-words-phrases-19:
Peter Mark Roget, a London doctor with a passion for order, published his Thesaurus in 1852 after decades of private lists. The 1911 edition is the classic form, the one scholars cite. Roget arranged English words by meaning rather than by spelling.

His system sorts the whole vocabulary into six great classes and 1,000 numbered idea groups. Writers use it to find the right word by starting from the thought. Roget's name became the word for the book itself, copied by many rivals since. Few reference works have shaped daily writing so quietly and so completely. Roget kept adding to his lists almost until his death at ninety.
nansen-northern-mists-vol1-1911:
In Northern Mists, from 1911, Nansen turned historian of the Arctic quest itself. Volume One runs from the Greek sailor Pytheas to the Norse voyages. The great polar explorer traces how the North was slowly found, imagined, and mapped.

Nansen sifts sagas, maps, and travelers' tales, testing each claim of early discovery. Vinland, the Irish monks, and the Greenland settlements all get his keen, skeptical eye. He writes as a sailor who knows ice and fog from his own decks. The volume remains a classic survey of early northern exploration, learned and readable at once. Old maps are reprinted so readers can test his claims for themselves.
nansen-northern-mists-vol2-1911:
Volume Two of Nansen's In Northern Mists, also 1911, carries the history of Arctic discovery from the late Middle Ages toward Cabot. Nansen the explorer reads the old records like a man checking a chart. Myths slowly give way to coasts that can be sailed.

He treats Marco Polo's northern hints, the fabled islands on portolan maps, and the search for a sea road to Asia. The volume weighs what the Norse truly found against what later ages claimed for them. Nansen's verdicts are careful and sometimes sharp. The two volumes together survey a thousand years of northern dreaming and discovery.
plos-pone-0003411:
Atsushi Honma, Koh-ichi Takakura, and Takayoshi Nishida modeled a trick of nature in this 2008 paper. In Batesian mimicry, a harmless species copies the warning look of a harmful one. Predators that learn the warning leave both species alone. The authors asked when smart hunting by predators helps this trick persist.

Their model used predators that forage in the most rewarding way. Such predators can favor the mimic sharing the model's protection. The mimic gains safety without paying the cost of being harmful. The work clarifies when copying a warning signal pays off in nature.
plos-pone-0003511:
William J. Tyler and co-authors stimulated brain circuits with sound in this 2008 study. Most brain stimulation uses implanted electrodes or light devices. Both routes are somewhat invasive for patients and animals. Ultrasound can pass through tissue without surgery.

Low-intensity, low-frequency ultrasound was used to excite neuronal circuits remotely. The sound reached its targets from outside the body. Such control yields large experimental and therapeutic power. The work opened a noninvasive path for brain research and care. Sound-based control would also spare patients the risks of brain surgery. It needs no implants and no drugs to work.
plos-pone-0003611:
ZhongQiang Chen, Omar S. Harb, and David S. Roos hunted parasite invasion proteins by computer in this 2008 paper. Apicomplexan parasites include Toxoplasma gondii and the malaria parasite. They invade host cells using specialized secretory organelles. Those small organs, like micronemes and rhoptries, release key invasion molecules.

The team's in silico screen predicted proteins for those organelles. They then validated hits in living Toxoplasma gondii. Computer prediction plus cell tests pulls hidden machinery into view. Secreted proteins are prime targets for drugs and vaccines. These parasites infect billions of people and farm animals across the world. The drugs against them are few, old, and often harsh on the patients who need them most of all.
plos-pone-0003711:
Lina S. V. Roth, Anna Balkenius, and Almut Kelber published this animal vision study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Horses are active by day and night, and they have some of the largest eyes of any land animal. The authors asked whether those eyes are sensitive enough to see colors in dim light.

They measured the absolute threshold of color vision in horses through behavioral trials. The tests find the faintest light at which colors can still be told apart. The result maps what the night world looks like to one of humanity's oldest working partners.
plos-pone-0003811:
Christina Nilsson, Anna Skoglund, Anthony P. Moran, and colleagues published this bacteria study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Helicobacter pylori settles in the stomach lining of half the world's people and stays for life. It is one of the most genetically diverse bacteria known, with new variants arising inside each host.

The team characterized single colonies to watch lipopolysaccharide diversity emerge within communities. Genetic changes in fucosyltransferase enzymes, which add sugars to the surface coat, drove the variety. The shifting surface sugars help this persistent colonizer stay ahead of the immune system.
plos-pone-0003911:
Carlos Prieto, Alberto Risueño, Celia Fontanillo, and co-authors built a map of human genes that switch on together in 2008. Microarray studies often hunt for such coexpression patterns across the genome. Most large studies, though, had not centered on human tissue samples. The team set out to build a network from human data.

Their PLOS ONE article draws on gene activity profiles from many human tissues. From them, they derived a network they judged trustworthy. Genes that rise and fall together often share jobs in the body. A solid human map helps researchers guess what unstudied genes do.
plos-pone-0004011:
Marco Canepari and Kaspar E. Vogt studied calcium signals in cerebellar neurons in 2008. Parallel fibers contact Purkinje neurons across long stretches of the cerebellum. Those contacts can trigger local calcium spikes in the branches. Whether such spikes cause lasting synaptic change was the question.

Their PLOS ONE article links dendritic spikes to a form of long-term potentiation. They report spikes saturate the cell's own calcium buffer. Freed calcium then helps set the lasting change. The work decodes how spatial patterns in fibers become stored signals. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004111:
Alexandra P. Rose presented an automated way to watch tree swallow nests in 2009. Studying how parents provision chicks has been limited by observation costs. Human watchers cannot cover whole days or long nestling periods. Attendance data therefore stayed patchy for many species.

Her PLOS ONE article describes automated monitoring of nest attendance. The method records visits across full days without a watcher present. With it, she measured time and individual variation in provisioning. Better data sharpen studies of how parents divide feeding work. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004211:
Jun Hayakawa and colleagues published this gene therapy study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The team had earlier reported on transplantation in two HIV-positive recipients, one of whom received retrovirus-modified blood stem cells meant to confer resistance to HIV. A key safety question for such therapy is where the retrovirus lands in the genome.

Here they report a long-term analysis of those retroviral integration sites in the treated patient. Tracking integration sites over years shows whether inserted genes stay quiet or disturb their neighbours. The follow-up is the kind of patient safety evidence gene therapy must produce.
plos-pone-0004311:
Juan Fargallo and colleagues published this ecology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Most ideas about how predators limit small mammal numbers come from northern, boreal ecosystems. There, many predators specialise on voles, and predator-prey systems are simpler than in the south.

The team studied kestrels and their prey in a Mediterranean region instead. They weighed the effects of generalist predation and climatic factors on the dynamics between the falcons and their food. Their work tests whether northern rules about predators and prey hold under a Mediterranean sun. The Mediterranean setting is the point: warmer, drier, and more varied.
plos-pone-0004411: In 2009, Esue, Tseng, and Wirtz found cell scaffolds stronger when paired. Alpha-actinin and filamin cooperatively stiffened long actin networks. The two linkers multiplied each other's strength. The neat finding maps the cell's skeleton mechanics. The neat teamwork explains cell rigidity well.
plos-pone-0004511: In 2009, Sussman, Mieog, and Doyle caught a germ bleaching corals. A Vibrio zinc-metalloprotease switched off coral endosymbionts and lesioned tissue. The bacterial enzyme dimmed the symbionts' light use. The finding names a true coral killer. The disease threatens reefs worldwide.
plos-pone-0004611: In 2009, Altaba warned that tree shapes can easily mislead. Global glitches skewed kinship tree branching, not global scaling laws. The tricky number guesses fooled pattern hunters badly. The short paper cautions tree experts strongly. The surface likeness is purely skin-deep.
plos-pone-0004711: In 2009, Tremblay, Robinson, and Costa built a lean model for wild animal tracks anew. A parsimonious approach to modeling animal movement data was developed. The simple model beat speed filtering soundly. The study aids ecology research. The tracking is growing fast.
ibsen-collected-works-archer-vol-11:
Archer's eleventh and final Ibsen volume gathers the last plays: Little Eyolf, John Gabriel Borkman, and When We Dead Awaken, in 1908 translations. Guilt, age, and the unlived life haunt all three. An old man facing death wrote these spectral dramas, and they read like reckonings.

A drowned child accuses his parents in Little Eyolf; a ruined banker paces his room in Borkman, dreaming of lost empire. When We Dead Awaken lets a sculptor and his model count what their art cost their lives. The volume completes the English edition that defined Ibsen abroad. It also closes the career of the father of modern theater on a note of strange, cold beauty.
bancroft-history-us-vol-11:
Bancroft turns to the making of the Constitution in the first volume of his 1882 sequel on its formation. Delegates gather at Philadelphia in 1787 to rebuild a failing union. Their debates, kept half secret, invent a republic meant to last.

The old historian treats the Convention as the capstone of his life's work. State rivalries, bold plans, and wise compromises fill his account. He sees the founding as deliberate, almost sacred work. Readers meet Washington, Madison, and Hamilton in the act of design. Bancroft's fervor gives the dry work of framing laws the glow of national epic.
froude-history-england-vol-11:
After the Armada comes triumph in the eleventh volume of Froude's History, from 1865. Spain lies humbled at sea, and England stands exalted among the powers. Elizabeth sits at the very zenith of her glory as queen.

Froude savors the victory toward which his long narrative has built. Sea dogs raid, courtiers scheme, and the queen holds her state with cool mastery. He writes the moment when England became a great power in earnest. The volume glows with national pride, and its flowing style shows why Froude ranked as the most dramatic English historian of the Victorian age.
lagrange-mecanique-analytique-1811:
Joseph-Louis Lagrange builds mechanics without a single diagram in Mecanique analytique, Volume One, in the 1811 edition. The whole of dynamics flows from one deep principle in his hands. Lagrange boasts in his preface that no figures will be found in the work, only algebra of the purest and most general kind.

Statics and dynamics gain a unity no earlier writer had reached. His methods still anchor how physicists treat motion and force today. The prose in French is calm, spare, and quietly proud throughout. Many call it the most elegant physics book ever written, a cathedral of reason raised on the work of Newton and his heirs.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-11:
Side by side, the Huron and Quebec missions run through Volume 11, from 1898. Thwaites sets the later 1630s on two fronts of one shared enterprise. While Brébeuf builds among the Hurons, the St. Lawrence colony takes shape below.

Letters from bark chapels sit beside reports from the river towns. Both tell of scarce food, hard travel, and slow gains in faith. The writers count each baptism and mourn each early death. Year by year and letter by letter, the record keeps its march. It shows French America's bold age from two ends at once.
journal-of-discourses-vol-11:
Volume Eleven, from 1865, greets the Civil War's end from Utah's pulpits. Young reads the slaughter as the nation's chastisement, long foretold. The prophet who warned of judgment now watches it fulfilled.

Vindication brings no triumph in the sermons' sober, watching tone. Speakers turn the Saints toward building, gathering, and the years ahead. The republic counts its dead while the mountain kingdom endures intact. Old prophecies get reread in light of smoking battlefields back east. The discourses close one age of warning and open one of patient work. Grief for the nation mixes oddly with pride in Zion's peace.
florio-italian-1611:
John Florio published Queen Anna's New World of Words in 1611, a greatly expanded Italian-English dictionary. Florio taught languages at the court of James the First and had already issued a smaller word book in 1598. The new volume, dedicated to Queen Anne, carried some 46,000 Italian words explained in English.

Entries give rich clusters of English equivalents, along with proverbs and phrases from Italian writers. Florio also translated Montaigne's essays, and his word-hoard fed the English of his age; scholars still debate his links with Shakespeare's circle. The dictionary was the first full bridge between Renaissance Italy and Jacobean England. Students of both languages still consult it for words that later books dropped.
bakunin-oeuvres-vol5-1911:
Volume 5 of Guillaume's Bakunin edition appeared in 1911, gathering the writings of the revolutionary's last great campaigns. By 1870 Bakunin was old and ill, but the Franco-Prussian War and the Paris Commune drew him back into action. He even joined a failed rising at Lyon, hoping to spark a wider revolt.

The texts include his appeals for a commune in Lyon and his letters and drafts from the Commune's brief life in Paris. He argued that war and empire had to be answered by revolution from below, not by new governments. The volume shows the old rebel's energy undimmed at the end of his active life. Guillaume's edition moves toward its close with Bakunin still, in his editor's phrase, in full cry.
brentano-aristoteles-weltanschauung-1911:
Franz Brentano published his study of Aristotle and his worldview in German in 1911. Brentano, the Austrian philosopher who revived the close study of the mind, had lectured on Aristotle for decades. He found his own leading ideas, above all the mind's direction toward objects, foreshadowed in the Greek master's texts.

The book follows Aristotle's development through the stages Brentano saw in his career, from early promise to mature system. It treats the soul, knowledge, and the divine mind as Aristotle's texts present them. Brentano reads the ancient philosopher as a living thinker rather than a museum piece. The study carried his reading of Aristotle to a new generation, including students who would reshape twentieth-century philosophy.
simmel-philosophische-kultur-1911:
Simmel gathered his essays as Philosophical Culture in German in 1911. The volume is his most readable book, the one where his gift for finding deep meaning in surface things shines brightest. Simmel wrote essays the way other philosophers wrote systems, one bright subject at a time.

The pieces treat Rodin the sculptor, Goethe the poet, the handle of a vessel, fashion, and the inner life of the modern city. Money, which his great Philosophy of Money had analyzed, returns here in essay form. Each piece begins with something small and opens onto the whole structure of modern culture. The book shows why Simmel's lectures drew crowds in Berlin: he made sociology an art form. Readers new to Simmel are still advised to start with these essays.
vinogradoff-growth-of-the-manor-1911:
Vinogradoff published The Growth of the Manor in 1911, his second great study of medieval England. The manor, a lord's estate worked by dependent tenants, was the seedbed of English rural society for centuries. Vinogradoff asked where it came from, and his answer reached back to Rome.

He follows the manor from possible Roman roots in the villa, through the free village communities of the early English, to its feudal prime under the Normans. The lord's hall becoming the manor court is the story's turning point, as custom hardened into jurisdiction. His evidence is charters, surveys, and court rolls, handled with famous precision. The book dug to the roots of English society and settled questions scholars had argued for a generation. It stands beside his Villainage as a foundation of manorial studies.
cotgrave-french-english-1611:
Randle Cotgrave published his Dictionarie of the French and English Tongues in 1611, the first great French-English dictionary. Cotgrave served as secretary to a great lord and spent years gathering French words from books and speech. His England was learning the tongue of Montaigne and needed a bridge between the languages.

The dictionary gives French words with generous English equivalents, proverbs, and turns of phrase, often with a flash of humor. It records the spoken French of its day beside the literary language, which makes it a treasure house of early modern speech. Four hundred years on, it remains a foundation of French study in England. Scholars of Shakespeare's age use it to catch meanings that modern French has lost, and students of both tongues still delight in its riches.
