frus-1945-50-intel-d111:
Ladd of the FBI wrote to Hoover on 14 May 1946. Ladd's memoranda kept the director informed on the bureau's intelligence fronts, the central group among them. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

By May the CIG under its new leaders was reaching toward the Latin American field the FBI regarded as its own. Ladd's paper belongs to the bureau's watch on that reach. Readers following the FBI thread can see its method again: steady reporting, claims restated, and a director who answered encroachment with paper of his own. The border war between the bureau and the group, fought in memoranda, is one of the volume's most instructive threads.
frus-1945-50-intel-d211:
A memorandum dated 17 April 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Eddy). The reader was Acting Secretary of State Acheson. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 211, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The first peace-time setup paired the National Intelligence Authority at the top with the Central Intelligence Group below it.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d311:
A memorandum dated 7 September 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was Robert P. Joyce of the Policy Planning Staff. The reader was the Counselor of the Department of State (Kennan). Readers meet it as document 311 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d411: A short paper dated 19 January 1950 carries only the heading Memorandum for the Record, with no writer and no reader named. It is document 411 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Papers of this kind set down what was said or decided at a meeting. The file would then hold it, even when no order followed from it.
frus-1861-d11:
On 16 July 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Baron von Gerolt, Prussia's minister in Washington. Gerolt was Prussia's minister in Washington. The letter is document 11 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

A letter to a foreign envoy in Washington worked the home end of diplomacy. Seward used such talks to press the Union's view of the war on each court through its own man. This exchange with Prussia's envoy sits just before the first great battle at Bull Run. Prussia's weight in Germany made its envoy a man worth the Secretary's direct time.
frus-1861-d111:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Anson Burlingame on 13 April 1861. Burlingame was named the American minister to China that spring. The letter is document 111 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The China post lay half a world away, yet it drew a letter the day after Fort Sumter fell. Seward had to keep every post filled, near or far, as war began. His note to Burlingame shows the wide reach of the service in that first week. Burlingame became a famed envoy in China and died in its service years later.
frus-1861-d211:
Mr. Wood was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 5 September 1861. It stands as Document 211 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d311:
Word from Mr. Harris reached Washington on 9 July 1861, in a letter to William H. Seward. It stands as Document 311 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d11:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 31 January 1862. It stands as Document 11 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It was written in the winter of the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d111:
Orders from Washington reached Charles Francis Adams in a State Department letter dated 28 July 1862. It stands as Document 111 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d211:
Writing on 6 March 1862, Lord Lyons addressed Secretary of State William H. Seward in a note printed as Document 211 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Lyons served as Britain's minister in Washington through most of the Civil War.

March opened the war's great spring campaigns, and within days the ironclads Monitor and Virginia would fight at Hampton Roads. A battle with loud echoes in naval capitals. British officials followed American events with care. Notes like this one, formal and to the point, carried the legation's business while the war widened around it. Stuart had served at the legation for years before he took charge of it.
frus-1862-d311:
Two Seward dispatches to Paris are dated 19 September 1862, and the first is Document 311 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both went to William L. Dayton, the American minister to France.

Seward wrote two days after Antietam, with the battle's scale known but its meaning still argued over. For Paris, the key fact was that Lee's invasion had been stopped. Seward's paired letters that day carried Washington's account to the French capital. There, the truce plan's fate depended heavily on how the Maryland campaign was read. Paris and London consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d411:
On 21 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Gustav Koerner, the American minister in Madrid. The dispatch is Document 411 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

By October 1862 the fighting at Antietam had slowed talk of foreign intervention, and Lincoln had announced his emancipation plan. Koerner's work in Spain shifted toward keeping that gain: holding Madrid to neutrality and watching Cuba, where Spanish rule sat close to Confederate shores. Seward's instruction belongs to the autumn effort to turn a military reprieve into lasting diplomatic safety for the Union.
frus-1862-d511:
August 1862 opened at The Hague desk with this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to James Shepherd Pike, dated 4 August. It is Document 511 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

August was the month of the second call for troops and of rising talk in London and Paris about stepping between the combatants. Seward's orders stiffened his ministers against any hint that the Union would accept mediation. Pike, in a small and friendly capital, had the easier version of that task, but the line had to be identical everywhere. The dispatch shows the Department keeping its whole European front in step as the war entered its most dangerous diplomatic season.
frus-1862-d611:
George G. Fogg, the American minister in Switzerland, received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 March 1862. It is Document 611 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, opening the Swiss file.

Switzerland was a small republic whose example Americans liked to cite and whose neutrality was absolute. Fogg, a New Hampshire editor and abolitionist, held the post at Berne. Orders to such a mission dealt with the standing courtesies and the war's presentation in a friendly, watchful little state. The dispatch begins one of the volume's shortest files. It is a reminder of the Department's reach. That care extended to every flag under which an American minister served, however quiet the post.
frus-1862-d711:
From Washington on 6 October 1862 came this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Andrew B. Dickinson. Dickinson was the American minister in Nicaragua. The letter is document 711 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, answering Dickinson's September reports.

Seward's answers gave envoys their marching orders and told them how Washington read their news. For Nicaragua, the transit route and the republic's steadiness sat at the heart of the brief. This letter is one turn in that exchange. It shows the State Department keeping its grip on a distant post whose ground mattered far more than its size.
frus-1863p1-d11:
William H. Seward sent this second letter of 8 December 1862 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 11 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, right after its twin. The two letters split the day's London business between them.

A secretary's mail often came in such pairs: one letter for the record of a talk, one for fresh orders. Seward's sheets to Adams kept the legation in step with a government whose war news changed by the week. Read beside document 10, this one shows the grain of that work — brief, plain notes that added up to a policy.
frus-1863p1-d111:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward a second time on 6 March 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 111 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The mate to a same-day letter often held the overflow: a talk in full, a set of facts, a press view. Adams's pair of 6 March fits that mold. This letter is its second half, sent as the ship fights in Britain's yards grew warm. With its twin, it shows the London brief at full stretch in the first week of spring.
frus-1863p1-d211:
Washington's orders to London on 5 June 1862 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 211 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Seward's orders set the line Adams had to press on the British government. They told him what to demand, what to soften, and when to wait. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d311:
Mr. Stuart, an officer of the British legation in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 November 1862. His note is document 311 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Small cases fill this part of the volume: a vessel, a cargo, a British subject under arrest. Together they show how a war at sea kept landing on diplomats' desks. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d411:
The American answer to London on 6 March 1863 took the form of this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 411 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

For historians, this exchange shows Anglo-American tension being managed day by day. It is the paper record of a war that never happened between the two countries. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d511:
A letter of 14 May 1863, from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, stands as document 511 in the printed record. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports.
frus-1863p1-d611:
Document 611 in the volume is a letter of 13 August 1863 from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
plos-pbio-0020211:
Juergen Tautz, Shaowu Zhang, Johannes Spaethe, and their team tested how honeybees judge distance in PLOS Biology in 2004. Bees tell nestmates how far food is through their waggle dance. To do that, a bee must measure the trip, a skill called odometry, based on how the world streams past its eyes.

The team flew bees over varied ground and watched how their estimates changed. Rough, rich scenery made trips feel longer than smooth ground did. That fits an eye-flow measure rather than energy spent. The study shows a tiny brain solving a navigation task with a simple, robust rule, a result that interests both biologists and robot designers.
plos-pone-0000111:
Donatella Bulone, Laura Masino, David J. Thomas, and their team studied protein clumping in PLOS ONE in 2006. Stretches of repeated glutamine, called polyQ, appear in several brain disease proteins, like the one in Huntington's disease. The longer the stretch, the more readily the protein clumps into toxic fibers.

The authors show the protein around the stretch matters as much as the stretch itself. The right context can delay clumping by holding the protein in a store of early, loose clumps called protofibrils. That delay changes how the disease clock might run. It also suggests a therapy idea: stabilize the harmless store, and the toxic fibers may never form.
plos-pone-0000211:
José M. Pérez, Iván L. Calderón, Felipe A. Arenas, and colleagues published this microbiology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Potassium tellurite is a compound long known to poison bacteria, used for over a century to select them in the lab. Yet why it kills was an old puzzle, an ancient enigma, as the title says. The authors work on how tellurite harms bacterial cells.

Tellurite still appears in microbiology labs and in some industrial settings. Pinning down its toxic mechanism explains both its killing power and how some bacteria resist it. The paper brings modern molecular tools to a question that dates back to the early days of bacteriology.
plos-pone-0000311:
Victor Frak, Isabelle Croteau, Daniel Bourbonnais, and colleagues published this motor control study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Prehension is the act of reaching and grasping. The authors report that merely simulating a grasp, imagining or preparing the action, modifies actual prehension. This is evidence that the brain represents an object's graspable features together with the action of grasping it.

Mind and hand share one representation, in this account. That joint coding explains why thinking about a grip changes the grip itself. The finding matters for rehabilitation and for understanding how the brain plans skilled movements.
plos-pone-0000411:
Patrick Peretti-Watel and colleagues examined how stigma against people with HIV may feed the epidemic in France, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Discrimination can push people to hide their status, avoid testing, or skip care. The team gathered evidence on how common such discrimination is and how it connects to the spread of HIV.

If fear of mistreatment keeps people from knowing or sharing their status, the virus gains room to spread unseen. Documenting that chain matters for policy: fighting stigma becomes part of fighting the epidemic itself, alongside medicine. The study grounds that argument in French survey and social evidence rather than assumption.
plos-pone-0000511:
Christopher B. Guest and colleagues studied how diabetes changes the way immune cells swallow fat, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. In artery walls, cells called macrophages gorge on stored cholesterol, known as cholesteryl ester. They swell into the foam cells of artery plaques. The team found this fat swallowing is turned up in macrophages from diabetic mice.

Two surface sensors, CD36 and SR-A, do most of the swallowing. Diabetes sharply raises heart disease risk, and fat-stuffed artery cells are a strong suspect link. Naming the sensors that do the work gives drug makers clear targets. The study ties a whole-body disease to a cell's appetite, tested one sensor at a time.
plos-pone-0000611:
Bernhard Voelkl and Ludwig Huber tested what monkey imitation really copies, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Marmoset monkeys watched a demonstrator perform a novel technique to get food. The team examined imitation as faithful copying of the novel technique: whether the observers reproduced the method itself, not just the result.

True imitation, copying actions rather than outcomes, is a milestone in the evolution of learning and culture. Marmosets are cooperative breeders with rich social lives, a promising place to look for it. Careful tests matter because animals often appear to imitate while actually using simpler tricks, and telling the difference defines what social learning means.
plos-pone-0000711:
John F. Bruno and Elizabeth R. Selig measured how coral cover has declined across the Indo-Pacific, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Many factors had recently caused mass coral deaths in all the world's tropical oceans. Yet little was known about the timing, rate, or spatial variability of the loss. The Indo-Pacific holds a major share of the world's reef-building corals.

The authors set the region's figure at 75 percent of the world's reef-building coral territory, making its trend the global story. Their analysis covers timing, extent, and comparisons between subregions. A firm baseline matters for conservation: without knowing how fast cover fell, no one can tell whether protection is working.
plos-pone-0000811:
Sanjay Chandriani and Don Ganem sorted the host's responses during aggressive infection by a cancer-linked herpesvirus, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Lytic infection by Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus brings an extensive shutoff of host gene expression. The shutoff runs chiefly through accelerated messenger RNA turnover, driven by the viral SOX protein, which destroys host messages. A small number of host mRNAs had previously been found to escape or rise.

By measuring host transcript accumulation during infection, the authors reveal several classes of host responses. Some genes resist the shutoff, others are actively induced. Those classes point to defenses the cell mounts, and to host factors the virus cannot do without.
plos-pone-0000911:
Stephen Proulx, Sergey Nuzhdin and Daniel Promislow looked for direct selection on genetic robustness in yeast, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Theory says living things should evolve ways to keep a healthy form despite shocks from outside or from their own mutations. Several routes to that steadiness were already known.

What was missing was proof that selection acts on robustness itself, not just on traits it protects. Reading the yeast transcriptome, the full set of active genes, the authors argue the signature is there. The claim matters for how we think traits stay stable over generations. It also bears on why some mutations stay hidden until stress reveals them.
plos-pone-0001011:
Joachim Goedhart, Joop Vermeer, Merel Adjobo-Hermans and colleagues built new glowing protein pairs to detect a doubled immune factor, in PLOS ONE in 2007. FRET is a technique where one glowing protein passes energy to another when they sit very close. The classic pair uses blue and yellow green fluorescent proteins.

Newer red shifted proteins could work better, with less background. The team built FRET couples from them and used the pairs to detect homodimers of p65, two copies of an immune control protein joined together. Better probes mean cleaner live cell images of proteins meeting. That feeds many fields at once.
plos-pone-0001111:
Matthew Witt and Brendan Godley used ship tracking data to map fishing at sea scale, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Saving marine ecosystems needs a full picture of fisheries alongside maps of biodiversity. The UK government's vessel monitoring system tracks large UK registered fishing vessels by satellite.

Witt and Godley investigate patterns of fishing activity in that data. Knowing where effort concentrates, season by season, is the base layer for seascape scale conservation, protecting whole seascapes rather than single spots. Fishing maps also expose where protected areas would bite and where they would merely displace boats. The paper shows a surveillance system doubling as a science tool.
plos-pone-0001211:
Growing tissues in three dimensions, rather than as flat layers, is a goal of tissue engineering. Takuya Matsumoto and colleagues demonstrated a patterning method in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their system uses a strained fibrin gel, a gel made from a blood-clotting protein, pulled so its fibers align.

The authors show three-dimensional cell and tissue patterning in the strained gel. Cells placed in such a scaffold can be guided into organized arrangements that mimic real tissue. Techniques like this are valuable both for studying how cells behave in tissues and for building cell and matrix composites for repair.
plos-pone-0001311:
In regions where malaria is seasonal, some people carry the parasite at very low levels. The levels are too low to see under a microscope. Those hidden infections can restart transmission. Badria El-Sayed and colleagues ran a randomized, open-label trial in eastern Sudan, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Treating these symptom-free carriers could be a useful way to control malaria.

The trial compared artesunate plus sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine with the same regimen plus primaquine. The goal was to clear sub-microscopic P. falciparum infections and gametocyte carriage. Gametocytes are the parasite stage mosquitoes pick up. Their comparison tests whether adding primaquine clears the reservoir better.
plos-pone-0001411:
Jairam Lingappa and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on couples where one partner has HIV and the other does not. Most HIV spread in Africa occurs in such couples, who often do not know their state. These couples face a high rate of new infection. The team mapped how common such couples are by region.

They also tracked how many joined a trial of ways to block spread. Rates of mixed state couples varied a lot from place to place. That spread shapes where trials and care will do the most good. The data help aim scarce funds at the couples and regions at highest risk.
plos-pone-0001511:
Guido Michels and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on the heart's pacemaker current. A set of channels drives the steady beat of the heart. Those channels were thought to have helper proteins that tune them, but few helpers were known. The team tested one such helper, called KCR1, in heart cells.

They show KCR1 curbs the pacemaker current and so slows heart rhythm. A brake on the beat is as vital as the drive itself. Faults in such brakes could underlie rhythm ills that now lack a cause. The work names a fresh target for rhythm drug research.
plos-pone-0001611:
Laura Wilding Crawford and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on pancreas shape faults in mice. A decade of work had named many factors that build the pancreas. Yet how its islets, the insulin hubs, take their right shape was still not known. The team read gene use in a mouse model where islet shape goes wrong.

Their gene lists flag paths that steer islet form as it grows. Faults in shape can blunt insulin release even when cells are present. That makes shape a real part of diabetes, not a side note. The lists give labs set leads for the next round of mouse tests.
plos-pone-0001711:
Ben Lopman and Simon Gregson reconstructed the history of HIV in Harare, Zimbabwe, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. HIV prevalence there had recently begun to fall, driven by high AIDS mortality and fewer new infections. To understand that turn, officials need to know when new infections, or incidence, peaked, and that date cannot be observed directly.

The authors used back-calculation, working backward from mortality statistics to infer past incidence. The full text gives the death data, the model, and their estimate of the peak year. Dating the peak helps judge which prevention efforts and behavior changes actually bent the epidemic's curve in one of the countries hit hardest by HIV.
plos-pone-0001811:
Laura D. Mydlarz, Sally F. Holthouse, Esther C. Peters, and their co-authors studied immune cells in sea fan corals in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Climate warming is making marine and land organisms, and even humans, more susceptible to emerging diseases. Coral reefs are among the ecosystems most impacted by climate stress, and coral immunity is ancient, inherited from the earliest multicellular animals.

The team examined granular amoebocytes, coral immune cells, and how they react to pathogen and climate stressors. The full text gives the cell responses under each stress. Knowing how coral defenders behave under heat and infection may help predict reef die-offs and protect the species that respond best.
plos-pone-0001911:
Ningli Cheng and co-authors tested how three genes interact in blood cancer in mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. One gene, Bcl-2, can slow cell death, which can help cancer grow, yet in some settings it slows cancer instead. A second gene, p27, acts as a brake on cell division, and a third, Bax, pushes cells to die.

The team bred mice lacking the p27 brake, with or without changes in the other two genes, and watched for T-cell lymphoma. As the title states, loss of p27 teamed with Bcl-2 to drive the cancer, but not with Bax. Gene pairs, not single genes, set the risk here.
plos-pone-0002011:
Christian Voigt and co-authors asked why Amazon bats visit mineral licks, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Many tropical animals in Africa, Asia, and South America trek to salt or mineral licks to eat clay or drink clay-rich water. Two ideas compete: the clay adds scarce nutrients to the diet, or it soaks up plant toxins the animals eat.

The team studied bats of the Amazon rainforest that visit such licks. Food or detox: each idea makes unlike predictions about which bats come and when. Settling the question explains a striking habit and what it says about nutrient limits in rainforest food webs.
plos-pone-0002111:
Dennis Hansen, Christopher Kaiser, and Christine Muller applied a classic ecology model to endangered island plants, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The Janzen-Connell model states that plant-specific enemies, such as seed-eating pests, hit offspring hardest close to the mother tree. Most past tests asked how the model explains diversity in rich forests.

The trio turn it to a practical aim: seed dispersal and establishment of endangered plants on oceanic islands. They also discuss ecological analogues, stand-in species that can take the role of extinct seed carriers. Old theory, put to work for conservation on islands that have lost their dispersers.
plos-pone-0002211:
Wook Kim and co-authors checked whether common mitochondrial lineages raise prostate cancer risk in Korean men, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Mitochondrial DNA is inherited from the mother and does not shuffle between generations, so its lineages, called haplogroups, are clean markers of ancestry. Some studies had hinted that mitochondrial variation might link to cancers, including prostate cancer.

The team compared haplogroups between patients and healthy men in the Korean population. They found no association between the common lineages and prostate cancer. A solid negative answer still helps, since it tells future studies to look elsewhere for the genetic roots of this cancer.
plos-pone-0002311:
Chris Paffen, Marnix Naber, and Frans Verstraten asked where in the brain a visual flip begins, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In binocular rivalry, the two eyes receive different images at the same spot. Perception alternates: only one image is seen at a time, then it switches. The phenomenon is a clean tool for studying how conscious perception is selected.

The team traced the spatial origin of a perceptual transition, the moment one image gives way to the other. Finding where the switch starts helps decide whether rivalry is settled in early visual areas or by higher decision centers. The answer bears on how the brain resolves any conflicting input.
plos-pone-0002411:
Ross-Ibarra and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Jeffrey Ross-Ibarra, Stephen I. Wright, John Paul Foxe, among others. Its subject is patterns of Polymorphism and Demographic History in Natural Populations of Arabidopsis lyrata. Many of the processes affecting genetic diversity act on local populations.

However, studies of plant nucleotide diversity have largely ignored local sampling. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002511:
Hadjantonakis joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Anna-Katerina Hadjantonakis, Elinor Pisano, Virginia E. Papaioannou, among others. Its subject is tbx6 Regulates Left/Right Patterning in Mouse Embryos through Effects on Nodal Cilia and Perinodal Signaling. The determination of left/right body axis during early embryogenesis sets up a developmental cascade that coordinates the development of the viscera.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002611:
Kitamura led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Masahiro Kitamura, Keisuke Nakashima, Yusuke Kowashi, among others. Its subject is periodontal Tissue Regeneration Using Fibroblast Growth Factor -2: Randomized Controlled Phase II Clinical Trial. The options for medical use of signaling molecules as stimulators of tissue regeneration are currently limited.

Preclinical evidence suggests that fibroblast growth factor (FGF)-2 can promote periodontal regeneration. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002711:
Ellen Kreijveld and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was immunological monitoring of renal transplant recipients to predict acute allograft rejection following the discontinuation of tacrolimus. Authorship is credited in the record to Ellen Kreijveld and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Transplant patients would benefit from reduction of immunosuppression providing that graft rejection is prevented. It goes on to note a further point. We have evaluated a number of immunological markers in blood of patients in whom tacrolimus was withdrawn after renal transplantation. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002811:
Laurent Gillet and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on the murid herpesvirus-4 gL regulates an Entry-Associated conformation change in gH. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Laurent Gillet, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The glycoprotein H (gH)/gL heterodimer is crucial for herpesvirus membrane fusion. It goes on to note a further point. Yet how it functions is not well understood. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002911:
Rufin VanRullen, Alvaro Pascual-Leone and Lorella Battelli studied a motion illusion with brain stimulation in 2008. A steady turning pattern can at times look as if it spins the wrong way. Such reversals have been taken as proof that motion vision works in discrete snapshots, though other accounts exist.

vaisesika-sutras-sinha-1911:
Nandalal Sinha translated the Vaisesika Sutras of Kanada into English in 1911. Kanada founded the Vaisesika school of Indian philosophy in ancient times. His sutras argue that everything reduces to eternal atoms combining under unseen law.

Earth, water, fire, air, minds, and souls all get sorted into categories. The system lists qualities, actions, and relations with rigorous care. Atomism was therefore born in India as well as in Greece. Sinha's edition includes commentary helping readers through the compressed aphorisms. The Vaisesika later merged closely with the Nyaya school of logic. Sinha's translation made this rigorous ancient physics available in English.
marie-de-france-guigemar-mason-1911:
Eugene Mason translated Marie de France's Guigemar into English in 1911. Marie wrote her lais, short Breton tales in verse, in the twelfth century. Guigemar stands first among the twelve lais she composed.

A hunting accident wounds the knight Guigemar in the thigh. A magical ship with no crew carries him to a foreign shore. There a lady, locked away by her jealous husband, heals and loves him. A knotted shirt and a belt serve as tokens of their fidelity. Separation and recognition close the tale in Marie's delicate manner. Mason's translation introduces the twelfth century's great woman poet to English readers gently.
marie-de-france-equitan-mason-1911:
Marie de France's Equitan, translated by Eugene Mason in 1911, is a lai of adultery punished. King Equitan of the Bretons falls in love with his seneschal's wife. The seneschal is his loyal right-hand man and closest companion.

The lovers plot to kill the husband in a boiling bath. Equitan himself is forced into the scalding water instead and dies. The wife follows him into the same bath in the tale's grim justice. Marie draws the moral that evil planned for others falls on the planner. Mason's translation keeps the sting of her irony. The short lai shows Marie at her most crisp and unforgiving.
marie-de-france-fresne-mason-1911:
Fresne, the Ash Tree, is among Marie de France's tenderest lais in Mason's 1911 translation. A lady slanders a neighbor for bearing twins, then bears twins herself. Fearing the same charge, she abandons one baby at an ash tree.

A porter finds the child, and nuns raise her behind convent walls. The girl, called Fresne for the ash, grows into a lord's beloved. Her twin sister's wedding finally reveals the truth of her birth. A brocade cloth and a ring serve as the recognition tokens. Hidden birth and love recognized close Marie's delicate tale. Mason's English keeps its gentle, forgiving tone throughout.
marie-de-france-bisclavret-mason-1911:
Bisclavret, the Were-Wolf, is Marie de France's great medieval werewolf tale in Mason's 1911 translation. A Breton nobleman vanishes three days each week without explanation. His wife presses him until he confesses his secret.

He turns wolf each week and must hide his clothes to return human. The wife betrays him to a lover, who steals the clothing. Trapped as a wolf, Bisclavret lives gently at the king's court. The king's hound and the wolf's own behavior reveal the truth at last. Treachery, loyalty, and the beast within drive the lai. Marie treats her werewolf with surprising sympathy throughout the tale.
marie-de-france-lanval-mason-1911:
Lanval is Marie de France's most Arthurian lai, in Eugene Mason's 1911 translation. Sir Lanval, a poor foreign knight, receives little favor at Arthur's court. A fairy mistress chooses him in secret and enriches him.

She forbids him ever to speak of her love to anyone. Queen Guinevere then propositions Lanval and, when refused, accuses him falsely. Forced to defend himself, he breaks his vow and names his mistress. The fairy lady rides into court and vindicates him before all. Love on trial frames the tale's bright, strange climax. Mason's version keeps Marie's sparkle in this favorite among her lais.
marie-de-france-deus-amanz-mason-1911:
Deus Amanz, the Two Lovers, is Marie de France's bleakest lai in Mason's 1911 translation. A king in Normandy sets a brutal condition for his daughter's marriage. Any suitor must carry her up a steep mountain without resting.

A young lover accepts the test and obtains a strength potion beforehand. Pride makes him refuse the drink when the climb grows hard. He reaches the top carrying her, then dies of the effort. The lady dies of grief beside him on the summit. Love's cruel arithmetic governs the short, sad tale. Mason's translation preserves Marie's restraint, which makes the ending hurt more.
marie-de-france-laustic-mason-1911:
Laustic, the Nightingale, shows Marie de France in miniature in Mason's 1911 translation. Two knights live as neighbors, and one loves the other's wife. The lovers can only talk through adjoining windows at night.

They claim their meetings are for listening to the nightingale sing. The jealous husband traps and kills the bird in revenge. He hurls its small body at his wife, staining her dress with blood. She sends the dead nightingale to her lover as a final message. He keeps it cased in a jeweled vessel forever afterward. Love, spite, and a dead bird fill Marie's shortest perfect tale.
marie-de-france-milun-mason-1911:
Milun is Marie de France's lai of patience rewarded, in Mason's 1911 translation. The famous knight Milun loves a lady he cannot marry openly. Their son is sent away to be raised by his aunt.

For twenty years a swan carries secret letters between the lovers. The swan flies the messages hidden under its feathers, year after year. The grown son becomes a champion and unknowingly faces his father in combat. Recognition comes through Milun's ring before either man is harmed. Father, mother, and son finally unite after the long separation. The swan post never fails in Marie's most patient love story.
marie-de-france-chaitivel-mason-1911:
Chaitivel, the Dolorous Knight, is Marie de France's lai of love's cost in Mason's translation. Four accomplished knights all love one lady in Brittany. She cannot choose among them and keeps all four hopeful.

A tournament turns festive rivalry into real disaster for the suitors. Three knights die, and the fourth is maimed for life. The survivor proposes the lai be named for his sorrow. The lady instead argues it should bear her own grief's name. Marie leaves readers to judge whose loss runs deeper here. The debate over the title becomes the poem's true subject. Mason's 1911 translation closes Marie's set with this thoughtful, melancholy piece.
marie-de-france-chevrefoil-mason-1911:
Marie de France wrote short verse tales called lais in the twelfth century, and Chevrefoil is her smallest one. Its subject is Tristan and Iseult, the famous doomed lovers of medieval romance. Eugene Mason turned the poem into English prose in 1911.

Banished from court, Tristan cuts a message for Iseult into a hazel branch left beside her road. The sign works like the honeysuckle wound round the hazel tree. Neither plant can live once the two are pulled apart. In just a few pages the tale says all it needs about love that cannot be parted, even by exile or death.
marie-de-france-eliduc-mason-1911:
Eliduc is one of the lais of Marie de France, the twelfth-century poet who wrote short verse tales of love and magic. Eugene Mason translated it into English in 1911. Its knight hero is torn between his wife at home and a new love across the sea.

Eliduc's second love falls into a deathlike sleep, and grief seems certain to win. Then a weasel wakes its dead mate by laying a red flower on it. Eliduc uses the same flower, and the shock of grace that follows changes every life in the tale. All three end by taking holy orders.
marie-de-france-yonec-mason-1911:
Yonec is a lai by Marie de France, the twelfth-century writer of short verse tales about love and the strange. Eugene Mason made this English version in 1911. Its heroine is a young wife locked in a tower by an old, jealous husband.

A knight reaches her window in the shape of a hawk, and the two become lovers in secret. The husband sets a trap, and the hawk-knight dies of his wounds. Their son, Yonec, grows up hearing the hidden story. When he learns the truth, he takes up his father's sword and settles the debt in blood.
lai-graelent-mason-1911:
Graelent is an anonymous Breton lai about a knight and his fairy mistress. Tales like it were told at medieval courts across France and Britain. Eugene Mason translated this one into English in 1911, alongside other lais of the same kind.

The fairy lady gives Graelent love and wealth, but she sets one hard rule. He must never speak of her to anyone. At court he breaks his word, and she vanishes. To win her back he must chase her through fountain and forest, past a white stag, in a pursuit that tests whether love can survive a broken promise.
conte-ponthieu-mason-1911:
The Count of Ponthieu is an anonymous French tale from the age of the Crusades. It calls itself a story of beyond the sea. Eugene Mason translated it into English in 1911, in a volume of old French tales of love and war.

Its heroine, the count's daughter, is seized while traveling and carried off overseas. A Saracen emir falls in love with her and treats her with honor. Around her gather questions of ransom, faith, and conversion. The tale shows how medieval Christians imagined the Muslim world they fought, feared, and sometimes admired.
chatelaine-de-vergi-mason-1911:
The Châtelaine de Vergi is an anonymous French tale from medieval Burgundy. It is short enough to read at one sitting, and it ends in grief. Eugene Mason translated it into English in 1911 with other tales of its period.

A knight loves the châtelaine in secret, and the secret itself keeps them safe. A jealous duchess drags the confidence out of the duke, her husband. One whispered word follows another until the trust is broken in public. The lovers die of the betrayal, and few medieval tales punish a loose tongue so harshly.
lai-lespine-mason-1911:
L'Espine is an anonymous Breton lai, a short medieval tale of knights and fairy folk. No author is known for it. Eugene Mason translated the French text into English in 1911, when he gathered several of these old tales into one volume.

A young knight rides out to a thorn tree at night, drawn by a challenge and a strange summons. There he crosses into the land of the fairy king. Mortal rules stop working in that place, and wonder turns quickly to danger. The tale is brief and eerie, told in the spare way of the old Breton storytellers.

arxiv-2606-16011: Large language models sometimes change their answers when challenged — but how easily, and by whom? This paper tests whether models flip their answers under counterarguments, comparing pressure from the model itself versus pressure from a different model. It finds answer instability is real and measurable, which matters for anyone building AI systems that must stick to correct conclusions.
arxiv-2606-16111: AI agents that use tools — search engines, calculators, code runners — face tradeoffs: faster but less accurate, or slower but better. This paper trains such agents with Pareto-ranking policy optimization, aiming for agents that sit on the Pareto frontier: the best possible balance where no goal can improve without hurting another.
arxiv-2606-16211: Answering biomedical questions often requires hopping across several papers and databases. BioMedHop is a benchmark testing that multi-source reasoning, and BioWeave is a framework that weaves evidence from many sources together to answer. The paper gives the medical-AI community both a test and a method for evidence-grounded answers.
arxiv-2606-16311: In game theory, some games mix discrete choices (build or not) with continuous ones (how much). This paper asks when such mixed-integer games have "rational equilibria" — stable outcomes where every player's strategy is a clean, rational choice rather than a messy mix. The authors characterize the conditions, targeting game-theory and optimization researchers.
arxiv-2606-16511: Evaluating language models often comes down to the "tail" — rare failures and edge cases. This paper argues tail-shape estimation in LLM evaluation is fragile, prone to false alarms, and offers a protocol for diagnosing those false positives. It targets AI evaluators who want benchmarks that don't cry wolf.
arxiv-2606-16811: Teaching AI to reason usually needs tons of hand-labeled examples.
